sentences.text: It was still dark when they left.
Isla had woken Camila before dawn, and they had eaten cold bread standing in the kitchen.
Abuelo was still asleep, though his fever was worse.
He had not woken up when Isla had put a cool cloth on his forehead.
She had left a note by his bed just in case, and a jug of water.
They had put on their thick sweaters and their wool caps and their boots.
Isla carried the notebook wrapped in a piece of oilcloth, and a canvas bag for gathering, and a small folding knife that Abuelo had given her for her tenth birthday.
Camila carried a smaller canvas bag and a paper bag with two apples.
The walk to the north corner was five kilometers.
In summer it took two hours.
In autumn, after weeks of rain, it took longer, because the paths were muddy.
Isla figured they would be there by nine, back by one, and could start the tea by two.
That would give Abuelo his first dose in the afternoon.
It was a plan.
She kept saying the plan to herself.
It made her feel less afraid.
The forest at the north corner was a temperate rainforest, thick and wet and green in every direction.
Everything dripped.
Everything smelled like moss.
The trees were pale and the ferns were huge, and Isla and Camila walked in single file along a narrow trail.
Isla went first, holding the notebook open in one hand.
Every so often she stopped to check a plant, in case it was the yerba de San Juan.
Most of them were not.
"How do we know it," Camila asked, after they had been walking a while.
"Small leaves," Isla said, reading.
"Dark green.
Little purple flowers, but only some of the year.
Grows near stones.
Smells like — Abuela wrote 'like a house after the rain'.
I don't know what that means." Camila thought.
"Like our house?
After it rains?
It smells like wood." Isla said, "I think so.
I don't know."
They found it at maybe ten o'clock.
Camila was actually the one who saw it — a small dark green cluster of leaves near the base of a big mossy rock, with three tiny purple flowers still holding on despite the season.
Isla checked the drawing.
The shape was right.
The color was right.
The purple flowers were right.
Camila leaned down and smelled the leaves.
She sat back on her heels.
"It smells like our house," she said.
"It really does.
It smells like wood." Isla smelled it too.
Camila was right.
It smelled like wood after rain.
"That's it," Isla said.
Her hands were shaking a little.
She was relieved.
She had been so afraid it would not be here, or that she would not know it.
But it was here, and she knew it.
"Now we have to sing to it," said Camila.
Isla had not been looking forward to this part.
She was not sure why.
She flipped in the notebook to the song.
It was written in Abuela's small careful notation.
There were four lines.
Isla could read music a little — she had learned some at the village school — but not well.
She hummed the first line under her breath, slowly.
Camila listened.
Camila did not need the paper.
Camila closed her eyes, and after a moment, she began to sing.
She sang the song in her small clear voice.
It was very simple — a low tune, four lines, in the old language of the island.
Camila had heard it maybe two or three times when Abuela had been alive.
She had remembered it.
She sang it now, kneeling in the moss beside the plant.
Isla did not sing with her.
She only listened, and she looked at the plant.
When Camila was done, Isla cut the plant carefully — not all of it, just what she needed, leaving the roots and some of the leaves so it would grow back.
That was another thing Abuela had taught them.
Never take more than half.
Never take from a plant that is alone in its spot.
Never take without asking.
Isla put the leaves in the canvas bag.
She said, quietly, "Gracias, hermana." She was not sure if she was talking to the plant, or to Camila, or to Abuela.
Maybe all three.
They found two more of the plants further along, near where a small stream came out of the moss.
They cut some from both — not too much, just a little from each.
Isla marked each place carefully in the notebook — a small dot on a hand-drawn map of the island, with the date.
Abuela had done the same thing for fifty years.
That was how Isla could tell where to look.
All the plants had dots.
By eleven o'clock they were walking back with a full canvas bag.
It was still overcast but it had not started raining hard yet.
Camila hummed the song as they walked.
She sang it to herself in a small voice.
Isla listened.
She thought, my sister is going to remember these songs longer than I am.
She thought, maybe that is what Abuela was doing, when she taught Camila the tunes first.
Maybe she knew that.
